subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The First Coffee Drinks
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The First Coffee Drinks.

hook.text: Early coffee wasn't brewed like today. People chewed the beans or boiled the whole fruit in water.

buildup.text: Ethiopian tribes mixed crushed coffee berries with animal fat to make portable energy balls.

discovery.text: Qishr, a drink made from coffee husks and spices, predates the bean brew and is still enjoyed in Yemen.

twist.text: Roasting beans and grinding them for brewing likely started in Yemen around the 15th century.

climax.text: That simple shift—roast, grind, brew—created the drink that would conquer the entire world.

punchline.text: Chewed fruit became a world-conquering beverage.

quiz.question: What is qishr?
options: A drink made from coffee husks and spices

details.summary: The earliest coffee beverages were not the filtered brew we know today. Yemenis and Ethiopians chewed raw berries, brewed cherry husks into a tea called qishr, or pounded dried berries into a paste. Roasting and grinding green beans into a brew came later and gradually became standard.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding early coffee drinks shows that what we call coffee today is just one of many possible preparations from the same plant. History could have gone differently.
takeaways: Early coffee was chewed raw or brewed from dried husks
Qishr, a cherry-husk tea, was an early popular drink
Roasting and grinding into brew developed gradually

faq.question: What is qishr and is it still consumed today?
faq.answer: Qishr is a spiced drink made from dried coffee cherry husks, often with ginger and cinnamon. It is still widely consumed in Yemen and parts of Ethiopia. Recently, the specialty coffee world has rediscovered it as cascara, marketing it as an upcycled byproduct of coffee processing.

faq.question: When did people start roasting coffee beans?
faq.answer: The practice of roasting green coffee beans likely began in Yemen or Turkey in the 1400s or 1500s. Roasting developed gradually as people discovered that heat transformed the hard green seed into something aromatic, grindable, and capable of producing the rich brew we now consider standard.
